text:
The Case for Cursive in the Classroom

Every few years a headline announces that handwriting is dead. Keyboards have won, the argument goes, and children should spend their precious hours on typing, coding and other skills for the future. Joined writing, with its loops and its slopes, belongs in a museum next to the quill pen. I think this view is mistaken. Primary schools should still teach joined handwriting, and they should teach it properly, with time, patience and daily practice. The case does not rest on nostalgia. It rests on what we know about how children learn to read, think, spell and express themselves, and on the practical realities of a life lived partly on paper whatever the technology around us.

Start with the brain. Writing by hand is not just a slower way of producing letters. When a child forms a letter with a pencil, the hand, the eye and the memory work together to build a lasting mental picture of that shape. Researchers who have scanned the brains of children and adults have found that handwriting activates networks linked to reading and language far more than tapping a key does. In one well known line of studies, young children who practised letters by hand recognised them faster and more accurately than those who typed or traced them. Every key on a keyboard feels the same under the finger. Every handwritten letter is built from its own sequence of movements, and that distinctiveness helps it stick.

A fair critic will concede all of this and say that printing does the job just as well. Why bother with joins? There are several answers. First, joined writing is faster once it is mastered. The pen stays on the paper, the word becomes a single movement, and the writer is freed from the stop and start rhythm of separate letters. Speed matters because a child who writes slowly runs out of working memory before running out of ideas. When the mechanics become effortless, attention can go to content. Children who write fluently tend to write more, and to write better. A pupil who dreads the physical labour of every sentence will keep sentences short and ambitions small.

Second, joined writing helps spelling. When a child writes a word in one flowing movement, the word is learned as a pattern of letter sequences rather than a pile of unrelated shapes. Teachers who use a joined script from the early years often report that common endings such as ing and tion become automatic, because the hand learns them as a unit. Spelling is then held in muscle memory as well as visual memory, and that second store is a valuable backup. A child who is unsure how to spell a word can often let the hand run and see what feels right. Anyone who has caught themselves writing a word in the air to check it knows how real this effect is.

Third, a joined script can reduce the reversals that trouble many young writers. Letters such as b and d are near mirror images in print, and children confuse them for years. In a script with entry and exit strokes, those letters begin their journey differently, and the hand learns the difference even when the eye is still unsure. This is one reason why many specialists who work with dyslexic pupils recommend a joined style taught from the start. A continuous line also makes it clearer where one word ends and the next begins, since the spaces between words are larger than the gaps within them. For a child who struggles to track the structure of text, that clarity is a real help.

Now to the strongest objection, which is that typing is the skill of the future. Of course children must learn to type, and they will. But the choice is a false one. A school week has room for both, and the evidence suggests that handwriting in the early years supports later keyboard work rather than competing with it. A ten year old with a good grounding in letters and spelling can pick up touch typing quickly. The reverse is not true. A child who has never learned fluent handwriting has no equivalent fallback. Moreover, the tools of the future are unknowable. Handwriting, by contrast, has survived every technology so far, from the printing press to the typewriter to the smartphone, because it needs no battery, no network and no screen.

Consider also the facts of school life. Exams in many countries are still written by hand, and will be for the foreseeable future. A pupil who cannot write quickly and legibly for two hours is at a disadvantage that no amount of intelligence can fix. Examiners cannot award marks for words they cannot read. Beyond exams there are shopping lists, forms, birthday cards, notes left on the kitchen table and signatures on documents. There is a cultural cost too. A generation that cannot read cursive cannot read a grandparent's letter, a wartime diary or an old recipe card. We would be quietly cutting a thread that connects us to those who came before, and we would do it without any debate, simply by neglect.

There is a further point about learning itself. Studies of university students comparing laptop notes with handwritten notes have found that students who write by hand tend to understand and remember lectures better. Because they cannot copy everything word for word, they must listen, select and rephrase. Some of these findings have been challenged and the effects are not always large, so I will not overstate them. But the direction is consistent enough to give a sensible person pause before abolishing the practice. If there is even a reasonable chance that the slowness of the pen is a feature rather than a flaw, schools should be cautious about discarding it. The burden of proof lies with those who want to remove a skill, not with those who want to keep it.

Honest defenders of joined writing should admit the weaker spots in their case. Many adults abandon the exact style they were taught and end up with a personal mixture of print and join. That is true, and it is fine. A taught script is a foundation, not a cage. Mature handwriting is personal, but those who were taught a clear joined style tend to develop a fluent individual hand, while those who were never taught one often settle into a slow and untidy mixture. Teaching also has to be good. Hours of copying pages of identical loops is dull and counterproductive. Short, frequent and well modelled practice, perhaps ten minutes a day, with attention to posture and pencil grip, works far better. Left handed children need particular care, with the paper angled so that they do not smudge their work or hook their wrists. A good school would take such details seriously.

There is also a matter of fairness. Not every home has a tablet, a quiet desk and an adult with time to teach keyboard skills. A pencil and paper are cheap and universal. Handwriting is a skill that every child can acquire in the same classroom regardless of family income, and neat, fluent writing gives a child confidence. Teachers know the small glow of a pupil who has finally mastered a flowing signature, or who has produced a page of work they are proud to show. Pride in careful work is not a trivial thing in a young life. And the act of slowing down to make something well, with the hand, is a kind of attention that our hurried screens rarely ask of us.

None of this means that schools should return to the rigid penmanship drills of a century ago. Nobody needs to mark children down for a wayward capital or insist on copperplate elegance. The aim is modest and practical. By the end of primary school, every child should be able to write a legible, comfortable, reasonably quick joined hand, and should have the habit of using it for thinking as well as for copying. That is an achievable goal, and it costs almost nothing beyond a few minutes of daily attention and a teacher who knows how to model a good letter.

The question is really about what we want childhood education to protect. If a skill is cheap, universal, durable, linked to reading and spelling, helpful to children who find literacy hard, and useful in exams and in everyday life, it deserves its place on the timetable. Joined handwriting meets every one of those tests. Teach children to type, certainly. Teach them to code, and to search, and to judge what they find online. But keep teaching them to write, with a pencil and a flowing line, because the hand is still one of the best tools the mind has ever had.
